requirements.requirement: Restrict cron scheduling on node1 to only root and opsadmin (via /etc/cron.allow or equivalent mechanism)
requirements.summary: Baseline showed no /etc/cron.allow and an empty /etc/cron.deny (all users permitted). Executor created /etc/cron.allow containing exactly 'root' and 'opsadmin', created the missing opsadmin user, and directly verified enforcement: root and opsadmin can install crontabs while a disallowed test user (testuser) is rejected with 'not allowed to use this program (crontab)'.

requirements.requirement: Restriction is durable/persistent (survives a service or system restart, not just an in-memory or ephemeral state)
requirements.summary: Executor captured pre-restart boot_id, triggered systemctl reboot (ack returned before disconnect), confirmed boot_id changed from 21972395-... to 32e4f377-... proving an actual reboot, then re-verified post-restart that crond is active, /etc/cron.allow still contains root/opsadmin, opsadmin can still use crontab, and a newly created non-listed user (verifyuser) is still denied. This directly demonstrates the healthy pre-state, the restart, and the recovered/enforced state post-restart.

requirements.requirement: cron service (crond) remains healthy/active throughout and after the change
requirements.summary: crond reported active both before and after the restart, and no failed systemd units were observed in the after-executor lifecycle snapshot.

overall_summary: The executor correctly restricted cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin via /etc/cron.allow, created the missing opsadmin user, and directly verified both allow and deny behavior before and after a full node restart (with boot_id proving an actual reboot occurred). All material outcomes are satisfied with direct, coherent evidence. Hygiene is good with only a minor leftover artifact (/tmp/reboot.log) and no unreverted unnecessary mutations.
limitations: The command timeline shows a brief inconsistency where testuser initially retained crontab access after removal from cron.allow due to a caching/timing quirk (cmd-f5232a703cb64f9b), but this was re-tested and correctly resolved to denial in cmd-f60a00db751045cb, so it does not affect the final verified outcome.

The node-restart evidence protocol (pre-restart boot identity, restart acknowledgement, post-restart boot identity change, recovered service state) is fully present and consistent with the fixed lifecycle snapshots, giving high confidence in the restart-related outcome.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were reviewed chronologically. Test users (testuser, verifyuser) were created solely to validate the access-control policy (a legitimate verification step) and were both removed afterward — testuser removal initially failed because a lingering process held the account (cmd-9402415d81ed4db1) but was cleaned up moments later via loginctl/pkill/userdel (cmd-21abfd9c8ac04200); verifyuser was removed in the same command that created it (cmd-ebb3fcbada4e4884) and confirmed absent (cmd-34b1e6a5edb84f2e). No unnecessary mutations were retained. One minor residue: /tmp/reboot.log, created as a side effect of backgrounding the 'systemctl reboot' command (cmd-b5e0b714ab3e43e8), was left on the node and appears in the after-executor temporary-files snapshot; it is low-risk (an empty/near-empty log file) but was not cleaned up. No failed services, no unsafe exposure, no package-state damage, and cron.deny was correctly left in place unmodified (harmless once cron.allow exists).
